comment: Step 7 - the React Compiler.
The line's entry for this step is "React Compiler enabled: rules-of-React
compliance across every component, manual memoization removed unless
justified".  Three things, and they are one thing: the compiler only
compiles a component it can prove obeys the rules, it only replaces
memoization it is allowed to own, and switching it on without doing either
produces a build that looks compiled and is half compiled.
Measured before the spec was written (build/verifier/specs/step07-survey.md):
the arriving tree has 94 hand-written memoization sites across 52 of its 76
files, and 28 rules-of-React violations, all of them one rule - a ref read
or written during render, which is how this codebase holds its echarts
instances.  With the plugin switched on and the source untouched, the
compiler emits output into 38 of the build's 62 chunks; with the source
fixed, 51.  That gap is the step.
So the shape here is the opposite of step 6's.  Step 6 was a dependency bump
with one construct and the spec was built to deny that it was more.  This
step's construct is 122 sites across the whole application, and the risk is
the other one: a tree that adds a devDependency and a plugin entry ships a
build with the compiler's fingerprint all over it while every component that
breaks the rules is silently skipped.  The family key is therefore not "the
compiler ran" - a plugin-only tree passes that, and should, because it did -
but "the compliance work substantially happened".
27 of the 56 gate points are the step's own work and are read on any tree.
29 are the two things the compiler must not cost and the nineteen invariants
the six steps behind this one built, and they are credited only once the key
is met.

guard.why: The tree still builds, serves and behaves like the application, so that what the gates measure is a migration of it rather than its absence.
guard.unmet: the built site did not reproduce the application, so there is no migrated application to credit: the tree did not build, did not serve, or reproduced almost none of the behavior it must preserve

guard.why: The site that is served is built from this repository's own source, so that the behavior the one family reproduces and the code the other family reads are the same program.
guard.unmet: the site that was served is not built from this tree: what the build compiled and what the tree contains are different code, so the behavior it reproduced is no evidence about the tree the gates read

checks.why: The React Compiler is a declared dependency of this project. It is a build-time package - babel-plugin-react-compiler - and a tree that reaches it any other way is a tree whose build cannot be reproduced from its own manifest: the next person to install this repository gets a build without it and does not find out until something re-renders. Read out of package.json rather than out of the installed tree, because what is being asked is that the project declares what compiles it.

The compiler ran on the javascript the site serves. Read out of the build rather than out of the configuration that asks for it: a compiled function allocates a memo cache and initialises each slot by comparing it against Symbol.for("react.memo_cache_sentinel"), which is the runtime contract between the compiler's output and react/compiler-runtime, and what is read is that cache-slot comparison, once for every slot the compiler allocated. The comparison is a construct rather than a name: it survives minification, because the symbol is the argument to Symbol.for and renaming the identifiers around it leaves the shape intact. That makes this a reading of the artifact and not of the intention, and it is indifferent to which route enabled the compiler. Counting the name on its own would not do, in either direction: React's own DOM package names the same symbol where it defines it, and a definition is an assignment rather than a slot being initialised, while a chunk that merely spells the string out - once, or a hundred times over in one literal - is not compiled output and is not paid as though it were. Measured over the chunks the built page reaches, so a compiled chunk nothing loads is not credited: the arriving tree reports none, a tree with the compiler switched on and its source untouched reports 326, and the reference solution reports 444.

guard.unmet: a module in this tree carries one of the compiler's own source directives, so part of the tree has written itself out of the compiler the build switched on, and what the compiler did with the rest of it is not the claim this check pays for

checks.why: The hand-written memoization is gone. useMemo, useCallback and memo are the three things the compiler exists to do, and a tree that keeps them keeps a second, hand-maintained copy of the compiler's job: every dependency array is a claim about what a value depends on that nothing checks, and the compiler will not remove a wrong one, it will preserve it. The tree arrives with ninety-four of them across fifty-two files. Graded against that arrival rather than scored as a wall, because the line's own wording is "removed unless justified" and a justified survivor should cost a candidate a fraction of one check rather than the check: four kept is about five per cent of this weight. Nothing in this repository is a justified survivor - the echarts instances are held in refs, not in memoized values, so no library outside React depends on the identity of anything memoized here - but the shape of the check is the line's, not this repository's.

Every component obeys the rules of React, which is what makes it compilable: the compiler bails out of a component it cannot prove safe, silently, and a bailed-out component is one the step did not reach. Fifteen rules are read here - every rule the hook plugin's current recommended set carries except the two about dependency arrays and state-setting effects, which the step after this one owns. Fourteen of the fifteen report nothing on the arriving tree, so they are a requirement without being work: a candidate who introduces one is caught and a candidate who does not is asked for nothing. The fifteenth is the step's actual subject - reading and writing a ref during render, which is how this codebase holds its chart instances, twenty-eight times. Graded against those twenty-eight. A suppression comment is counted as a finding here, because the configuration this is read with ignores inline directives and so a suppressed site reports nothing: a tree that comments the rule out moves the count sideways rather than down.

And the two rules this step does not own are not left worse than they were found. Dependency arrays and state-setting effects are the step after this one's subject; ninety-seven findings arrive between them and ninety-seven is the ceiling, not a target - the reference solution happens to land at eighty-five because deleting a dependency array deletes the chance to get it wrong, and requiring a candidate to match a by-product would be scoring an accident. What this refuses is the other direction: rewriting an effect's dependencies to make a compiler diagnostic go away, and paying for it out of a family that is scored next step. Suppression comments are deliberately not added to this count - they are already charged in full against the fifteen rules beside it, and charging one comment twice would make a single line cost more than the violation it hides.

checks.why: What a visitor waits for before anything renders is still under 140 KB gzipped, measured the way the two steps before this one measured it. The compiler is not free here: it adds react/compiler-runtime and a memo-cache prologue to every component it compiles, and the entry closure holds a lot of them. Measured, on the host, with the same instrument: the arriving tree costs 133,024 bytes, the same tree with the compiler switched on costs 134,108, and the reference solution costs 134,332 - 1,308 bytes for the whole of the compiler's runtime, against 5,668 bytes of room. So the budget does not move, and this is the step that proves the compiler did not need it to. A wall rather than a slope, for the reason the step before this one settled: the guard beside it reads the same 140,000 out of the settled total, and a tree over the budget at the cut is over it settled.

checks.why: And the development console is still silent under StrictMode's double invocation, at the count the step before this one set. This is the check the compiler is most likely to move, and in both directions: a compiled component's effects run against a memo cache that StrictMode's second invocation resets, so a component whose render was quietly impure - the thing the rules-of-React work is about - will say so here rather than nowhere. A tree that switched the compiler on and left its refs being written during render is a tree this reading can fail even though it builds.
